note.caption: Same penam nucleus; only the acyl group on position 6 differs.
body: Both drugs share the fused β-lactam and thiazolidine nucleus with its position 3 carboxylate. They differ only at position 6: a phenoxyacetyl group in penicillin V, a 2-amino-2-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetyl group in amoxicillin.
Penicillin V is relatively stable to gastric acid. Amoxicillin and ampicillin, which carry the side-chain amino group, brought improved activity against Gram-negative bacteria.

note.caption: Same β-lactam, fused to a five-membered or a six-membered sulfur ring.
body: Both bind penicillin-binding proteins through the same β-lactam. In amoxicillin it is fused to a five-membered thiazolidine ring; in cefuroxime, to a six-membered dihydrothiazine.

The cephalosporin core carries two variable side chains, R1 and R2, where a penicillin has one. Cefuroxime's R1 holds a methoxyimino group, a feature of the oxyimino cephalosporins developed to counter β-lactamases.

note.caption: Same benzimidazole sulfoxide core; OCHF₂ versus OCH₃ changes how fast acid activates it.
body: Both drugs link a pyridine and a benzimidazole through a sulfinyl bridge, and both are weak bases (pKa about 4) that are activated by acid. Omeprazole has a 5-methoxy on the benzimidazole and a 4-methoxy-3,5-dimethyl pyridine; pantoprazole has a 5-difluoromethoxy and a 3,4-dimethoxy pyridine.
The electron-withdrawing OCHF₂ makes pantoprazole slower to activate and more acid-stable, and it bonds Cys813 and Cys822 rather than Cys813 and Cys892.

note.caption: Simvastatin's lactone must open; atorvastatin already has the dihydroxy acid.
body: Both drugs inhibit HMG-CoA reductase through a 3,5-dihydroxy acid side chain. Simvastatin, a fungal-type statin, carries it closed up as a lactone and is a prodrug: hydrolysis opens the ring to the active hydroxy acid.
Atorvastatin is a synthetic statin with the acid already open, built on a pyrrole carrying a fluorophenyl and a phenyl amide instead of a naphthalene ester.

comparisons.title: Two ethyl ester prodrugs of ACE inhibitors

note.caption: Same ester prodrug trick; ramipril adds a cyclopentane ring to the proline.
body: Both drugs are dipeptides with one carboxylic acid capped as an ethyl ester. Hydrolysis of that ester gives the active diacids, enalaprilat and ramiprilat, whose carboxyl group binds the zinc ion of ACE.
The difference lies at the proline end: ramipril fuses a cyclopentane onto the ring. In the C-domain of ACE this adds hydrophobic contacts with Val379 and Val380.

comparisons.title: One biphenyl tetrazole, two different partners

note.caption: Both are biphenylyltetrazoles; valsartan swaps the imidazole for acylated valine.
body: Both molecules carry a tetrazole, an acidic stand-in for a carboxylic acid, on a biphenyl joined by a methylene to a second unit. In losartan that unit is a substituted imidazole. In valsartan it is open-chain: L-valine whose nitrogen bears a pentanoyl group, forming an amide.
Valsartan already has a carboxylic acid, whereas losartan gains one only when its hydroxymethyl group is oxidised to the metabolite EXP3174.

comparisons.title: Why one acetylates cyclooxygenase and the other does not

note.caption: Aspirin's acetyl sits on oxygen as an ester; paracetamol's sits on nitrogen as an amide.
body: Both drugs carry an acetyl group, but bonded differently. Aspirin's is an ester, which a serine of cyclooxygenase (Ser530) attacks, taking the acetyl and inhibiting the enzyme irreversibly. Paracetamol's acetyl is attached to nitrogen, forming an amide.

The routes proposed for paracetamol are different: as a reducing agent it lowers the peroxide tone that COX needs, and a central pathway runs via the metabolite AM404. Its mechanism is still not fully understood.
